items.name: Sleeping bag for an unheated apartment
items.need: If heat fails in winter, a warm sleeping bag lets each person stay warm in bed without burning anything indoors.
items.how_to_choose: Choose synthetic fill, because it keeps some warmth if it gets damp and is easy to wash. A rectangular or semi-rectangular cut is roomier and can double as a quilt on the sofa. Go by the comfort rating, not the number in the name: a bag sold as a '20' is often comfortable only to the mid-30s F. Look for a comfort rating of 32 F (0 C) or lower, or plan a blanket over the bag, and add a wool hat and a layer under you. Check packed size if closet space is tight.

qty.note: One bag for each adult and child. Not for a baby: a baby sleeps on a firm, flat surface of their own, never in a sleeping bag.

items.already_own: A good comforter plus a wool blanket on top, or any sleeping bag in the household, is enough for a mild cold snap. Test by sleeping in it in a cold room before you need it.

safety_notes.text: Hypothermia warning signs in adults are shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. In infants, look for bright red, cold skin and very low energy. A body temperature below 95 F is a medical emergency: get help, and warm the person while you wait.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

safety_notes.text: To stay warm indoors without heat: use extra blankets, close off unused rooms, block drafts at the bottom of doors, and close curtains at night. Check on older adults often because they may make less body heat.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

safety_notes.text: Fuel-burning heating can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless and deadly gas. Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas and test them monthly. Use portable generators outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the home. Keep electric space heaters 3 feet from anything that burns, plug them straight into a wall outlet and turn them off when you sleep.
safety_notes.source_title: Keep Warm and Safe This Winter: Tips for Using Generators, Furnaces and Space Heaters (Jan 23, 2026)

safety_notes.text: A sleeping bag is not for a baby. CDC says to put a baby to sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface, in a sleep area of their own such as a crib or bassinet in the room where you sleep, with soft bedding such as blankets and pillows kept out and the baby's head left uncovered.
safety_notes.source_title: Providing Care for Babies to Sleep Safely

items.name: Window insulation film kit (and draft stopper)
items.need: Single-pane and leaky windows lose a lot of heat; clear shrink film and a door draft stopper hold warmth in a room you heat with body heat or a safe electric heater.
items.how_to_choose: Pick a kit by window count and size, and check the tape is rated for your frame. Duck Brand says its tape is safe for renters on painted wood, aluminum and vinyl but not on plaster, drywall or unfinished wood. Film goes on the inside and shrinks tight with a hair dryer. For under doors, a long fabric tube filled with rice or sand, or a rolled towel, works as a renter-safe draft stopper; this page picks no draft-stopper product.

qty.note: One kit covers about 3-5 standard windows; add a second kit for a larger apartment.

items.already_own: Clear plastic sheeting plus painter's tape works in a pinch, and a rolled towel works as a draft stopper. A heavy lined curtain closed at night also helps.

safety_notes.text: To stay warm indoors without heat: use extra blankets, close off unused rooms, block drafts at the bottom of doors, and close curtains at night. Check on older adults often because they may make less body heat.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

item_flags: No lab insulation-value (R-value) test of any kit was found; reviewers judged installation, wrinkles and durability only.
Tape adhesive can mark unfinished wood, plaster and drywall (Duck Brand label). Test a small patch if you rent.
No draft-stopper product is recommended here; a rolled towel follows CDC's tip to block drafts at the bottom of doors.

items.name: Rechargeable or USB fan
items.need: A small fan keeps air moving in a stuffy apartment during a summer outage and runs from a battery or power bank, not the grid.
items.how_to_choose: Battery size and speed matter more than blade size. Outdoor Life measured runtime on high speed only; a low speed will last longer, but no test of it was found. Choose USB-C so one power bank can charge or run it. Avoid the cheapest clip fans that shut off on small power banks.

qty.note: One per household; more if people sleep in separate rooms.

items.already_own: Any USB desk fan works from a power bank. A 10,000 mAh bank (about 37 Wh) runs a 5 W fan for roughly 6-7 hours; check the fan's watt rating.

safety_notes.text: Fuel-burning heating can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless and deadly gas. Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas and test them monthly. Use portable generators outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the home. Keep electric space heaters 3 feet from anything that burns, plug them straight into a wall outlet and turn them off when you sleep.
safety_notes.source_title: Keep Warm and Safe This Winter: Tips for Using Generators, Furnaces and Space Heaters (Jan 23, 2026)

safety_notes.text: CPSC has recalled rechargeable fans because the lithium-ion battery can overheat while charging, for example Rite Aid handheld fans (July 2021) and IcyBreeze Buddy misting fans (September 2025, two fires). Charge fans where you can see them, not overnight under bedding, and check cpsc.gov/Recalls before buying.
safety_notes.source_title: IcyBreeze Cooling Recalls Portable Misting Fans Due to Fire Hazard

safety_notes.text: The 2021 Rite Aid rechargeable handheld fan recall: lithium-ion battery can overheat while charging; full refund.
safety_notes.source_title: Rite Aid Recalls Rechargeable Handheld Fans Due to Fire Hazard

items.name: Hard cooler (about 50 quart)
items.need: When the fridge warms in an outage, a cooler packed with ice keeps perishables at or below 40 F so you do not have to throw everything out.
items.how_to_choose: Ice retention matters, but so does what fits in an elevator and a closet. A 45-50 quart cooler is about 25-27 in long. Pre-chill it, fill it mostly with ice, and keep it closed. Test results vary a lot between publications because test conditions differ, so compare within one test. Both picks are 50 to 52 quarts and weigh about 15 to 31 lb empty, sized for the contents of a fridge. For refrigerated medicines alone (X7-02), any cooler that holds the medicine and a few frozen packs will do; a smaller one is easier to carry down stairs.
items.already_own: Any hard cooler with a tight lid works. Put a fridge thermometer inside it: food in a cooler follows the same rule as food in the fridge.

safety_notes.text: With no thermometer, treat fridge food as unsafe once the power has been off for 4 hours with the door kept shut. With a thermometer in the fridge, throw out meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers once they have been above 40 °F for more than 2 hours. Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or is at 40 °F or colder, can be refrozen or cooked. Never taste food to test it.
safety_notes.source_name: FoodSafety.gov (copy kept by the Porter County, Indiana, health department)
safety_notes.research_note: The original page, https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/food-safety-during-power-outage, returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch on 2026-11-15. The county's PDF copy of that page (date last reviewed 8 August 2024) was fetched and read instead. The wording is the owner's, from prompt 2.1. Listed in pending.json so the original can be opened in a browser.

safety_notes.text: CDC says that once the power has been out for 4 hours, refrigerated perishable food goes into a cooler, with ice or frozen gel packs added to keep it at 40 °F or below.

items.name: Low-wattage electric kettle
items.need: Hot water is an extra, not part of the plan: in an apartment every meal is planned to be eaten cold. If you own a power station that can run one, a small electric kettle heats water for drinks or instant meals with no flame indoors.
items.how_to_choose: Check the watts first: most power stations under 300 W of inverter output cannot run a kettle at all. Heating one quart takes roughly 95 to 115 Wh whatever the kettle's wattage, so a 300 Wh station gives only about two to three quarts, and a 300 W kettle needs at least 20 minutes per quart. Heat only what you need, put a lid on, and look for a UL or ETL mark on the kettle's label.
items.already_own: Any kettle rated at or below your power station's continuous output works, but a normal 1,500 W kettle will overload most small stations.

safety_notes.text: Never run generators, grills or camp stoves inside a home, garage or basement or near windows, and do not use a stove or oven to heat the home. Have a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

safety_notes.text: Fuel-burning heating can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless and deadly gas. Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas and test them monthly. Use portable generators outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the home. Keep electric space heaters 3 feet from anything that burns, plug them straight into a wall outlet and turn them off when you sleep.
safety_notes.source_title: Keep Warm and Safe This Winter: Tips for Using Generators, Furnaces and Space Heaters (Jan 23, 2026)

items.name: Sealed food storage bins
items.need: Stored rice, cans and dry goods stay dry and safe from mice, roaches and pantry moths in a bin with a real seal.
items.how_to_choose: Look for a gasket in the lid plus latches on both sides. Low bins (about 6-7 in) slide under a bed; taller ones go on a closet floor. Brittle polypropylene cracks in cold, so keep them indoors. Pests chew through thin plastic over time, so check bins monthly and keep food in its own packaging as well. Neither maker says its bin is made for food to touch, so keep food in its own packets or in lidded food containers inside the bin. Only the Budget bin, at about 7 in high, slides under most beds; the Standard bin is nearly 11 in high.

qty.note: Two bins to start; buy more if you store more than a few weeks of dry food. The Budget bin is sold in packs of three.

items.name: Manual evacuation stair chair
items.need: If someone at home cannot walk down stairs and the elevators stop, an evacuation chair lets trained helpers take them down a stairwell.
items.how_to_choose: Ask your building manager first: many high-rises already hold evacuation chairs and have a plan. Treat any chair as a candidate until you have read the current manual for the exact model. Check the maximum working load in the manual, not in the advert, against the person plus clothing and equipment, and ask the maker which test the figure comes from: the RESNA standard for these chairs, ED-1, was still a draft when checked. Have the supplier train the helpers on your own stairs.

qty.note: One per household that needs it; check with building management before buying.

items.already_own: Many buildings, especially high-rises and schools, already keep stair chairs and have staff trained to use them. Ask management and ask to be added to the evacuation list before you buy.

safety_notes.text: ED-1, the RESNA standard for emergency stair travel devices, sets performance and test rules (weight capacity, stability, dynamic load, maneuverability) and requires makers to publish dimensions and occupant weight capacity. The weight-capacity test uses a manikin equal to a 99th-percentile adult male, about 350 lb; heavier loads need added weight. Inspection is required at least every 12 months and after each evacuation or drill. The standard was out for public comment in 2025.
RESNA ED-1 is the standard for emergency stair travel devices used by individuals with disabilities; the RESNA page describes it as a final draft and gives no year.

item_flags: One candidate, not a pick: the Evacusafe Excel tracked evacuation chair, $1,795 at the maker's US store and 30 lb. The maker's product page and data sheet say it carries 500 lb, but the operating manual linked from the same page gives a maximum working load of 400 lb, and none names a test standard. Plan on the lower figure and ask the maker in writing which applies.

Before buying any chair, get the current manual for the exact model and have building management, the supplier and the person's occupational therapist or mobility specialist check the fit, the rated load, your stairs and landings, storage, upkeep and how many trained helpers it needs. Write down another way out, and the point at which the person leaves early, in case any of this cannot be met.
A chair alone does not make a stairwell safe: it needs trained helpers and practice, and a stairwell may be full of other people or smoke. This is this site's judgement, not an official source's.

items.name: Two-way radios (FRS / GMRS)
items.need: When phones and internet fail, handheld radios let family and neighbors talk within a building or a block.
items.how_to_choose: The minimum is two radios: one for each group that will be apart. Buy the same model for everyone so they share channels. FRS radios need no license; GMRS radios have more power but need a license. Claimed ranges of 25-35 miles are for open line of sight; in a city expect far less. No test of range inside concrete buildings was found: Outdoor Life measured about 0.3-0.6 mi with trees and hills in the way, and a concrete high-rise will cut that much further. Plan on a few floors or one building, not blocks, and test them before you need them.

qty.note: Two radios is the minimum: one for each group that will be apart. A two-pack counts as two; a radio sold singly is bought twice. Add one radio for each extra group.

items.already_own: Any FRS radios you own work with FRS-only radios on the same channel. Many cheap 22-channel radios are FRS/GMRS hybrids; use them only on FRS channels at FRS power unless you hold a GMRS license.

safety_notes.text: FRS radios need no individual license. GMRS needs an individual FCC license; one license covers the licensee's family members. Under the FCC's 2017 rule change, FRS power is 2 W on channels 1-7 and 15-22 and 0.5 W on channels 8-14, and radios sold as FRS/GMRS combinations are treated by power: above the FRS limit they are GMRS and need the license. (This is the 2017 fact sheet and draft order, so check the FCC's current pages for the fee and any later change.)
safety_notes.source_title: Part 95 Personal Radio Service Reform fact sheet and draft Report and Order, WT Docket 10-119 (Apr 27, 2017)

item_flags: Hybrid FRS/GMRS radios sold on marketplaces often claim long range and high power; the FCC treats combination radios above FRS power as GMRS, which needs a license.

No in-building range test was found. Outdoor Life measured about 0.3-0.6 mi with trees and hills in the way, and a concrete high-rise will cut that much further. Plan on a few floors or one building, not blocks, and test them before you need them.
